items.rationale: The dividing line is who owns the control flow: in a workflow, predefined code decides the sequence of steps; in an agent, the model decides its own steps and tool use. Counting model calls (a) or tools (c) does not separate them, since workflows can call a model several times and use tools, and the number of models (d) is irrelevant.

The model is called inside steps, but the code fixes the order and chooses each next step, so this is a workflow. Using a model and a tool (a) or taking several steps (b) does not make something an agent; the number of tools (d) is not the test.

When the steps are known and the same every time, code can enforce the order, which is more reliable and gives a predictable number of model calls and cost. Agents are the more flexible option, not workflows (b), and either can call tools in order (c, d).

items.answer: Code owns the control flow in the booking part, and the model owns it in the manual-question part.
accepted: The program decides in booking and the model decides for manual questions.
Booking is code-controlled; manual questions are model-controlled.
In booking the code decides the next step, in manual questions the model decides.
items.rationale: Full credit needs both halves the right way round: code for the fixed booking steps, model for the manual search. Reversing them, or saying the model owns both, is wrong. Giving only one half correctly is partial.

An agent pays off when the steps cannot be listed in advance, as in diagnosing a failed print, where each finding decides the next check. Booking (a), reminders (b) and opening hours (c) follow a known path and are better as fixed workflows, which are cheaper and more predictable.
Extra calls per request: 5 - 2 = 3. Over 1,000 requests that is 3,000 extra calls at $0.01 each, so $30. Answering 50 or 20 computes the cost of only one side instead of the difference.
